opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something we've thought about quite a bit. Right now Genie is made up of a few pieces: a video tokenizer that compresses frames into discrete tokens, a latent action model that infers what "action" happened between frames without any labels, and a dynamics model that predicts the next frame's tokens given the past and that latent action. We train the tokenizer first and then train the latent action model and the dynamics model together, so it's already partly joint, but not fully end-to-end.

The appeal of going fully end-to-end is pretty clear. In principle, each component could shape its representations around what the others need. The tokenizer might learn to keep the details that matter for controllability rather than just reconstruction quality, and the latent actions might become more meaningful if the gradients flowed all the way through. Modular pipelines also tend to compound errors: if the tokenizer throws something away, nothing downstream can recover it.

That said, there are real reasons we didn't start there. Training everything jointly at scale is harder to stabilize, especially with discrete bottlenecks like vector quantization in the loop. There's also the risk of collapse in the latent action model. If it isn't constrained, it can just smuggle information about the next frame through the action channel instead of learning a small, consistent set of controls. Separating the pieces gives us a lot more control over those failure modes, and it makes debugging much easier. When something goes wrong, you can tell whether the problem is reconstruction, action inference, or dynamics.

So I'd say it's very much a direction worth exploring, and I'd expect future versions of these world models to move toward more joint training as we understand the components better. The modular design was the practical way to get something working and to learn what each piece really needs to do. Once you have that understanding, it becomes much more feasible to fold the pieces together.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a question we get asked a lot, and honestly it's something we've thought about quite a bit. The way Genie is set up right now, it's really three components. There's the video tokenizer, which compresses frames into discrete tokens, there's the latent action model, which infers what action happened between consecutive frames in a completely unsupervised way, and then there's the dynamics model, which takes the tokens and the latent actions and predicts the next frame. And we train those somewhat separately, in stages.

So the question is, why not just do it all at once? And I think in principle there's no reason you couldn't. The appeal is obvious. You'd have a single objective, you'd avoid any mismatch between what the tokenizer learns to represent and what the dynamics model actually needs, and you could imagine the representations getting better because they're shaped end-to-end by the prediction task.

But there are a couple of reasons we didn't start there. One is just practicality. When you're scaling to tens of thousands of hours of internet video and models in the billions of parameters, being able to train and debug the pieces independently is a huge deal. If something goes wrong, you want to know which part of the system is responsible. The staged approach gives you that modularity.

The second reason is more about the latent actions specifically. The thing that makes Genie interesting is that the actions are learned without any labels. We're just watching video and asking the model to discover a small, discrete set of controls that explain the changes between frames. That's a delicate thing to learn. We found it really helps to have the latent action model trained with its own objective, with an information bottleneck, so that the actions end up being meaningful and controllable rather than just leaking pixel information from the next frame. If you fold that into one big end-to-end loss, there's a real risk that the model finds a shortcut, where the "action" just becomes a compressed version of the future frame, and then you lose the controllability, which is the whole point.

So my honest view is that the end-to-end version is a very natural next step, and I'd expect people to explore it. But I'd want to see that you can preserve the quality of the learned actions. If you can do that, and it simplifies the pipeline, great. If it just gives you a slightly better video model that you can't actually control, you've lost the thing that made it a world model in the first place.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s an interesting direction. You could imagine training the whole system together, so that the representation it learns and the dynamics it predicts are optimized for the same objective. But there’s a trade-off: separating those components gives you more control over what each one learns and makes it easier to understand where things are going wrong.

The question for me would be whether training end to end actually improves the things we care about. Does the model produce coherent environments over time? Can you reliably control what happens? Generating something that looks plausible is one part of it, but learning an environment you can interact with is a stronger requirement. So I’d see it as something worth exploring, rather than assuming a single model would necessarily be better.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a really interesting direction. Right now, Genie has these different components: you learn a representation of the video, you learn the latent actions, and then you learn the dynamics conditioned on those actions. Training those together could allow the representations to be shaped more directly by what the model needs to predict and control.

But there’s also a challenge in making sure the model actually uses the action representation. You don’t just want a model that generates plausible video; you want the actions to have a consistent effect on what happens. So I think an end-to-end approach is appealing, but you’d need to be careful about the training objective and how you preserve that controllability.
